intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honor all of them. Today's roll was seed 4197351998. Here is each roll and what came of it.

rolls.became: Why would a lighthouse freeze comets? Because a comet is just ice and dust that glows while it melts. Freeze one and it keeps its glow for later, like leftovers. Thaw it in the lamp and you get light. So Sallow catches them and keeps them in the cellar.
Comets fall at night, and you move a knitted net under them. The ones you miss land in the sea and wash up on the sandbar at dawn, still cold, so you can scoop those too.

A hundred years ago the Mariners' Almanac described the light at Sallow Point as “sallow by name, sallow by nature; adequate.” Sallow has not gotten over it. The meter is the Almanac's five stars, measured by how far away you can see the light.
Dawn. Comets only fall in the dark, the clock in the corner counts down to sunrise and ticks out loud for the last ten seconds, and every day the sun goes after whatever the cellar can't keep cold.
Sallow Point, and Sallow, the lighthouse that never shook off its own name.

rolls.value: a tech tree with exclusive choices
rolls.became: The lamp has seven lens rings, and each ring fits exactly one lens. That's why every choice is one or the other: Lure Lens or Twin Lens, Frost Lens or Glow Lens. Lenses are paid for in Shine, the light you make.

rolls.value: the core action goes obsolete; you manage automation
rolls.became: A billion comets need more hands than a lighthouse has. Sallow knits Wool Folk out of the old keeper's jumper, and they work hardest when nobody's looking, which is also why they keep working while you're away. Once the Rota Board goes up, the net is retired and you run the shifts: Nets or Lamp at night, Cellar or Beach by day. You ring the shift bell until they knit a rota of their own.

Each two-minute day is a whole loop of the game. At night you catch comets and the lamp makes Shine. By day the misses wash up and the sun thaws the cellar, which glows as it wastes them, and the crew has to be on the right shift for both.
Everything is cut from felt with a running stitch round the edge: comets are pompoms with yarn tails, the stars are cross-stitches, and the sea is yarn.

So the felt diorama is a synthwave poster: a striped sunset sun, a grid running off across the sea, pink, teal and gold. The soundtrack is soft synthwave in C major pentatonic, and every catch plays a note a step higher up that scale.
Plum night, coral and cream stripes, a mint cellar window, a teal sea and a yellow lamp.

Cozy-creepy: the comets knock from inside the cellar, the Wool Folk have the vanished keeper's initials stitched on their backs, the keeper's armchair is still warm since 1911, and the Surveyor has a lantern where a face should be.
Comets come down felted together in clumps, then clumps of clumps. By the end the cellar holds twenty billion of them.
About two hours over a few sittings, with three ways of playing: catching, running shifts, and watching the Wool Folk run themselves.

When the light is seen from the Almanac's office, the Surveyor arrives, crosses out the old entry and writes five stars and “very bright, actually.” Sallow asks about a sixth star (you might have written to ask already). There isn't one. So Sallow decides to thaw all twenty billion comets at once anyway.

rolls.value: one you have to be talked out of
rolls.became: The Surveyor, the gulls of Gull Rock and the Wool Folk each beg you not to. You insist three times, the night goes brighter than noon, and the whole shower goes back up into the sky. The Almanac's next edition: “Once, extremely.” The Fireworks Permit you bought for no reason covers it.

outro: None of these were chosen; all of them were rolled. The fun is finding the one story where they all make sense.
